[] It sounds like you’re going through a double dose of adjustment — losing a valued coworker and remembering the sting of losing a favorite player. In both cases, there’s an emotional connection and shared rhythm that’s suddenly gone.

One way to adjust is to actively create new points of connection in your environment. At work, maybe invite another colleague (or even two) to those coffee breaks, so it becomes a fresh tradition instead of an empty routine. It’s not about replacing your friend, but about expanding your circle to let in different kinds of positive energy.

Also, keep a few consistent rituals that bring you joy — whether that’s a Cubs game, your community projects, or your salsa nights — so part of your week still feels familiar and grounding.

And on the emotional side, give yourself permission to feel a little off. Transitions take time. Just like warming up before a game, let yourself ease into the new season of work life — the energy will come back once you find your new team dynamic.

[] I hear you — when work feels like it’s in extra innings every single day, even our go-to mood boosters can start to lose their magic. It sounds like your morning park run has been a key part of your recharge routine, so maybe it’s time to adjust the game plan a bit rather than retire it completely.

One approach is to mix up the sensory experience a little — try a different route through the park, shift the time to catch a sunrise, or bring along an energizing playlist (bonus points for baseball walk-up songs!). You might also layer in some quick mindfulness right after your jog — even two minutes of deep breathing before diving into the day can change how you carry that energy.

Off the field, making sure you’re getting enough rest, staying hydrated, and building in a few intentional breaks during the workday can help too. And if the stress keeps hitting line drives at you, maybe have a chat with your supervisor about workload — even star players need recovery days.

[] It sounds like you’ve really been in the middle of a busy stretch — and even the most energetic players need a breather between innings. Making time for moments like the one you described by the lake is great, because it engages your senses and slows down your mental pace. The key is to make those mini-pauses a regular part of your lineup, not just a rare pinch-hit.

A few ideas you could try:
- **Scheduled ‘quiet innings’**: Pick a couple of times each week where nothing is on the agenda — no calls, no errands, no emails. Protect them like you would game day.
- **Micro-breaks**: Even 10 minutes between tasks to go for a walk around the block or stretch in the sun can help prevent long-term fatigue.
- **Delegate or team up**: With community projects, see if there are tasks you can share with volunteers so you’re not carrying the entire lineup yourself.
- **Combine joy with restoration**: If you love being at the ballpark or the lake, pair that with restful activities like reading, light journaling, or just sitting quietly.

Remember — keeping yourself well isn’t dropping the ball. It’s making sure you can still swing for the fences when it counts.
